set1.q: Why is a patient with cardiomyopathy referred to cardiology?
opts: Only once symptoms occur at rest
Referral does not wait for symptoms at rest. It establishes care, considers genetic testing and reviews high-risk features early.
Only when a device must be implanted
Device decisions are one reason, but referral also establishes care, considers genetic testing and reviews high-risk features.
Only after an admission for edema
An admission is not required first. Cardiology referral is made to establish care and review risk, testing and treatment options.
To establish care and review risk features
Correct. Referral is to establish care, consider genetic testing, review any high-risk features, and discuss medications or the need for an intervention.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which group is particularly susceptible to acute myocarditis?
opts: Smokers
Smoking is not the susceptibility marker; young males are particularly susceptible, typically with no prior cardiac disease.
Young males
Correct. There is no race predilection and incidence is similar between the sexes, although young males are particularly susceptible.
Older women
Older, postmenopausal women make up most stress cardiomyopathy. In myocarditis it is young males who are particularly susceptible.
Infants
Infants are not the named susceptible group. Myocarditis particularly affects young males, usually otherwise healthy.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: How often is heart muscle biopsy useful in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Rarely; not used routinely
Correct. Biopsy is not used routinely and is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy; it is reserved for rapidly deteriorating function or systemic diseases that may involve the heart.
Always, to confirm it
Biopsy is not needed to confirm dilated cardiomyopathy; the echocardiogram, electrocardiogram and imaging carry the diagnosis, and biopsy is rarely useful.
Routinely, before drugs
Treatment does not wait for tissue. Biopsy is not used routinely in dilated cardiomyopathy and is kept for specific indications.
Yearly, for monitoring
There is no surveillance biopsy. Biopsy is rarely useful in dilated cardiomyopathy and is used only for defined indications.

set1.q: Which device therapies are part of adult cardiomyopathy care?
opts: Carotid stent or vena cava filter devices
These devices treat carotid stenosis and venous clot, not cardiomyopathy. Adult device therapy is a defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker.
Temporary external pacing, as needed
External pacing is not the listed strategy. Adults receive an implantable defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker when indicated.
Defibrillator or biventricular pacemaker
Correct. Adult device therapy is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker, with an assist device or transplant considered in advanced cases.
Intra-aortic balloon pump for all patients
A balloon pump is not listed as adult cardiomyopathy device therapy. The devices are a defibrillator or a biventricular pacemaker.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which laboratory results are typical of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: High lipase and amylase
Pancreatic enzymes are not the markers here. Troponin and B-type natriuretic peptide are elevated.
Raised troponin and peptide levels
Correct. Troponin I and T are usually elevated and B-type natriuretic peptide is frequently elevated, which adds to the resemblance to acute coronary syndrome.
Normal troponin, normal peptide
Normal markers would not fit. Troponin is usually elevated and B-type natriuretic peptide frequently elevated.
High ferritin and transferrin
Iron studies point to hemochromatosis, a restrictive cause. Stress cardiomyopathy raises troponin and natriuretic peptide.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: When is cardiac catheterization obtained in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Yearly, for surveillance
There is no routine catheterization surveillance. It is obtained before a planned pacemaker or surgery.
Before any beta blocker
Drug therapy does not need catheterization first. It is done when a pacemaker or surgery is planned.
Before a pacemaker or surgery
Correct. Catheterization is not required for diagnosis; it is obtained when invasive therapy, a pacemaker or surgery, is planned.
To make the diagnosis
Echocardiography makes the diagnosis. Catheterization is kept for when invasive therapy is planned.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Why may a permanent pacemaker be needed in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Outflow obstruction on exertion
Outflow obstruction is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The pacemaker in restrictive disease treats conduction disease from nodal fibrosis.
A low ejection fraction on echo
Systolic function is usually normal until late. The pacemaker indication is heart block from nodal fibrosis.
Recurrent atrial thrombus
Atrial thrombus is prevented with anticoagulation, not pacing. Pacemakers treat heart block from nodal fibrosis.
Nodal fibrosis causing heart block
Correct. Fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes can lead to heart block, so a permanent pacemaker is placed for conduction system disease.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which heart sound is often present in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: S4, from a noncompliant ventricle
Correct. An S4 heart sound is often present because the left ventricle is noncompliant; blood pressure and heart rate are usually normal and the apical impulse is forceful and sustained.
S3, from a compliant ventricle
The third sound comes from blood striking a very compliant, volume-overloaded ventricle, as in dilated cardiomyopathy, not a stiff hypertrophied one.
An opening snap after S2
An opening snap belongs to a stenotic mitral valve. The stiff ventricle of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy produces an S4.
An ejection click before S2
An ejection click is not the sound taught here. The noncompliant hypertrophied ventricle gives an S4.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: What is the diastolic abnormality of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without obstruction?
opts: Reduced compliance, high filling pressure
Correct. The hypertrophied myocardium resists diastolic filling (reduced compliance), and the elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure reflects that decreased compliance.
Increased compliance, low filling pressure
A compliant ventricle with low pressure is the opposite. Hypertrophy stiffens the ventricle and raises end-diastolic pressure.
Weak contraction and a huge cavity
A weak squeeze with a large cavity is systolic dysfunction of dilated cardiomyopathy; the hypertrophic problem is diastolic filling.
Pericardial fluid limiting filling
Fluid in the pericardial sac is cardiac tamponade. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the stiff, thick muscle itself limits filling.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Besides valve regurgitation, which complications does dilated cardiomyopathy put patients at risk for?
opts: Arrhythmias and thromboembolism
Correct. Rising end-systolic volumes drive further dilation and dysfunction, and patients are at risk for arrhythmias and thromboembolic complications.
Outflow obstruction and syncope
Outflow tract obstruction with syncope belongs to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where a thick septum narrows the subaortic outflow tract.
Heart block from nodal fibrosis
Fibrosis of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes causing heart block is a feature of restrictive cardiomyopathy, which may need a permanent pacemaker.
Plaque rupture and infarction
Plaque rupture is a coronary event; the definition of dilated cardiomyopathy requires the absence of severe occlusive coronary disease.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which side of heart failure often dominates in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Left-sided failure
Left-sided symptoms occur, but right heart failure often dominates in restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Neither side at all
Filling pressures are elevated in both ventricles, and right-sided failure is often the more prominent.
High-output failure
High-output failure is a different mechanism. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a stiff-ventricle disease with right-sided dominance.
Right-sided failure
Correct. Even though filling pressures are elevated in both ventricles, right heart failure is often more prominent: hepatomegaly, bilateral pedal edema and ascites.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Why is a high degree of suspicion needed to identify acute myocarditis?
opts: It only affects older adults
Myocarditis usually affects otherwise healthy people, especially young males. Suspicion is needed because cases are often not obvious.
Biopsy is never diagnostic
Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard. A high index of suspicion is needed because many cases are clinically subtle.
Many cases are not clinically obvious
Correct. Because many cases of myocarditis are not clinically obvious, a high degree of suspicion is required to identify it.
Troponin is always normal in it
Troponin indicates myonecrosis and can be elevated. Suspicion matters because many cases are not clinically obvious.

set1.q: What proportion of patients with mild myocarditis later develop dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Nearly all
Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely; only one third later develop dilated cardiomyopathy.
None
The risk is real: one third of patients with mild myocarditis later develop dilated cardiomyopathy.
One third
Correct. Most patients with mild symptoms recover completely, but one third subsequently develop dilated cardiomyopathy.
One half
Half overstates it. One third of patients with mild myocarditis later develop dilated cardiomyopathy.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which region does the hypertrophy of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy most frequently involve?
opts: Right ventricular wall
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a left ventricular disease; the region most often thickened is the interventricular septum.
Left atrial wall
The left atrium enlarges from high filling pressure, but it is not hypertrophied myocardium; the septum is the classic site.
Ventricular apex only
The apex can be involved because any region may be, but the most frequent site is the interventricular septum.
Interventricular septum
Correct. The hypertrophy is often asymmetric and can involve any region of the left ventricle, but it most frequently involves the interventricular septum.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: What are the most common symptoms of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Claudication and pallor
Claudication is a peripheral artery symptom. Stress cardiomyopathy presents most often with chest pain and dyspnea.
Fever and myalgia first
A febrile, achy prodrome precedes viral myocarditis. Stress cardiomyopathy presents with chest pain and dyspnea.
Ascites and pedal edema
Right-sided congestion dominates restrictive cardiomyopathy. Stress cardiomyopathy most often causes chest pain and dyspnea.
Chest pain and dyspnea
Correct. Chest pain and dyspnea are the most common symptoms; palpitations, nausea, vomiting and syncope also occur, and the examination is nonspecific.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Why must diuretics be used cautiously in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: They worsen iron overload
Diuretics do not affect iron stores. The caution is that stiff ventricles depend on preload to keep output up.
They thicken the walls
Diuretics do not change wall thickness. They must be used carefully because lowering preload drops cardiac output.
Stiff ventricles need preload
Correct. Diuretics treat pulmonary and systemic congestion, but they lower preload, and noncompliant ventricles depend on preload to maintain cardiac output.
They cause heart block
Heart block in restrictive disease comes from fibrosis of the conduction nodes, not diuretics; the caution is about lowering preload.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which serious outcome can the arrhythmias of acute myocarditis cause?
opts: Septal hypertrophy
Septal hypertrophy is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which is inherited, not a result of arrhythmia. Myocarditis can cause sudden cardiac death.
Pericardial effusion
An effusion is a pericardial problem. The arrhythmic danger in myocarditis is sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmia or block.
Sudden cardiac death
Correct. Palpitations, syncope or sudden cardiac death can result from underlying ventricular arrhythmias or atrioventricular block in acute myocarditis.
Aortic dissection
Dissection is an aortic wall problem, not an arrhythmic outcome. Myocarditis arrhythmias can cause sudden cardiac death.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which infection from beta-hemolytic streptococcus involves the heart in 50% to 90% of cases?
opts: Q fever
Q fever is a rickettsial cause of myocarditis. The beta-hemolytic streptococcal cause affecting the heart in 50% to 90% is rheumatic fever.
Rheumatic fever
Correct. Rheumatic fever, from beta-hemolytic streptococcus, affects the heart in 50% to 90% of cases and is among the infectious causes of myocarditis.
Lyme disease
Lyme disease is a spirochete infection that can cause myocarditis, but it is not streptococcal; rheumatic fever is.
Diphtheria
Diphtheria is a bacterial cause of myocarditis, but not a streptococcal one. The streptococcal cause is rheumatic fever.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which activity advice is given to patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Competitive sport if asymptomatic
Competitive, extreme exertion is what links to sudden death; activity is kept mild to moderate and noncompetitive.
Complete bed rest indefinitely
Bed rest is not advised. Mild to moderate noncompetitive recreational activity is allowed.
High-intensity interval training
High-intensity exertion raises sudden-death risk. The advice is mild to moderate noncompetitive activity.
Mild to moderate, noncompetitive
Correct. Patients have historically been told to confine themselves to mild to moderate recreational activity in a noncompetitive manner, since sudden death relates to extreme exertion.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which echocardiogram pattern fits restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Big atria, near-normal ventricles
Correct. The echocardiogram shows marked enlargement of one or both atria, near-normal left ventricular systolic function and cavity size, preserved ejection fraction and abnormal diastolic function.
Dilated, thin-walled ventricles
Dilated, thin-walled ventricles with reduced ejection fraction describe dilated cardiomyopathy.
Small cavity, septal bulge
A small cavity with septal hypertrophy is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not the restrictive pattern.
Apex akinetic, base normal
Apical and midsegment akinesis is stress cardiomyopathy, not the restrictive pattern.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: In dilated cardiomyopathy, which patients receive anticoagulation?
opts: Only patients whose cause is viral infection
The cause of the cardiomyopathy does not decide anticoagulation. Atrial fibrillation, artificial valves or mural thrombus do.
Atrial fibrillation, prosthetic valve or clot
Correct. Anticoagulants should be restricted to patients in atrial fibrillation, with artificial valves or with a known mural thrombus.
Every patient from diagnosis, lifelong use
Anticoagulation is not universal. It is restricted to atrial fibrillation, artificial valves or a known mural thrombus.
Any patient with a reduced ejection fraction
A reduced ejection fraction alone is not an indication. Anticoagulation is kept for atrial fibrillation, artificial valves or mural thrombus.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which drugs may benefit patients with restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Antibiotics, steroids or antivirals
These do not treat the stiff ventricle. Treatment targets the underlying disorder, with beta blockers or verapamil or diltiazem.
Beta blockers, verapamil or diltiazem
Correct. Beta blockers and the calcium channel blockers verapamil or diltiazem may help by lengthening filling time, improving relaxation and reducing sympathetic stimulation.
Digoxin, epinephrine or dopamine
Positive inotropes are not the benefit drugs here. Beta blockers or verapamil or diltiazem are the options listed.
Nifedipine, nitrates or hydralazine
These are vasodilators. The listed options are beta blockers and the calcium channel blockers verapamil or diltiazem.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: What characterizes restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Transient apical ballooning after stress
Transient apical and midsegment hypokinesis after a stressor is stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy.
Impaired filling, near-normal chamber size
Correct. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is impaired diastolic filling with reasonably preserved left ventricular chamber size and wall thickness normal or slightly increased.
Dilated chambers with thin, weak walls
Dilated, thin-walled chambers with poor contraction are dilated cardiomyopathy, a systolic disease.
Asymmetric septal thickening of 1.5 cm
Unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more, most often septal, is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which medication is a recognized cause of myocarditis?
opts: Amiodarone
Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic used in cardiomyopathy care, not among the drug causes of myocarditis such as methyldopa.
Methyldopa
Correct. Medications that cause myocarditis include penicillin, thiazide diuretics, tetracycline and methyldopa; toxins include lithium, arsenic, lead and copper.
Metoprolol
Metoprolol is a beta blocker used for outflow obstruction and heart failure, not a named cause of myocarditis like methyldopa.
Lisinopril
Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor used in treatment, not a cause. Methyldopa is the drug cause here.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which parasite causes dilated cardiomyopathy through Chagas disease?
opts: Toxoplasma gondii
Toxoplasma does not cause Chagas disease. Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted by triatomine bugs in Central and South America and Mexico.
Plasmodium falciparum
Plasmodium causes malaria, not Chagas disease. The parasitic cause of dilated cardiomyopathy is Trypanosoma cruzi.
Giardia lamblia
Giardia is an intestinal parasite with no link to Chagas disease, which is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and can end in dilated cardiomyopathy.
Trypanosoma cruzi
Correct. Trypanosoma cruzi causes Chagas disease, a parasitic infectious myocarditis that leads to dilated cardiomyopathy; it is spread by triatomine (kissing) bugs.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: How should suspected Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy be evaluated and treated at first?
opts: As acute coronary syndrome
Correct. Because it mimics acute coronary syndrome with no reliable early differences, evaluation and treatment follow established acute coronary syndrome protocols, with admission to cardiology.
As a panic attack at home
Sending the patient home ignores the resemblance to an infarct. Early management follows acute coronary syndrome protocols.
As viral myocarditis first
Myocarditis is managed supportively, but stress cardiomyopathy is handled as acute coronary syndrome until catheterization.
As restrictive disease
Nothing suggests restriction. The early approach is to follow acute coronary syndrome protocols.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: What do Kerley B lines on a chest radiograph indicate?
opts: Pulmonary edema
Correct. Kerley B lines are 1-2 cm horizontal lines meeting the pleura at right angles, and they indicate pulmonary edema; the film may also show cardiomegaly and effusions.
Pleural effusion
Pleural effusions can appear on the same film, but Kerley B lines themselves are short horizontal lines that indicate pulmonary edema.
Pneumothorax
A pneumothorax shows a lung edge with absent markings. Kerley B lines are short horizontal lines at the periphery that indicate pulmonary edema.
Lung fibrosis
Kerley B lines are not a sign of fibrosis in this setting; the short horizontal lines touching the pleura indicate pulmonary edema.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which self-care point is advised in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Stay well hydrated
Correct. Patients maintain hydration and avoid dehydration, which lowers preload and worsens obstruction, and they avoid excess alcohol.
Limit fluids strictly
Fluid restriction risks dehydration and lower preload, which worsens obstruction. Patients are told to stay hydrated.
Drink more alcohol
Excess alcohol is to be avoided. The self-care points are hydration and moderation of alcohol.
Use nitrates freely
Nitrates aggravate outflow obstruction and are avoided if possible. Hydration is the self-care point.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: Which echocardiogram finding confirms a clinical diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Apical ballooning with a normal base
Mid and apical wall-motion abnormality is the stress (Takotsubo) pattern, not hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Pericardial thickening on the images
Pericardial thickening points to constrictive pericarditis, best shown on cardiac magnetic resonance imaging.
Unexplained wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more
Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed by unexplained increased left ventricular wall thickness of 1.5 cm or more anywhere in the wall, most often asymmetric septal hypertrophy.
Ejection fraction under 35% with dilation
A low ejection fraction with dilated chambers points to dilated cardiomyopathy; ejection fraction is usually normal in hypertrophic disease.

set1.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set1.q: What does a normal electrocardiogram suggest when dilated cardiomyopathy is suspected?
opts: It has no value here
The tracing does carry value. It is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, so a normal electrocardiogram nearly excludes it.
It almost rules it out
Correct. The electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in dilated cardiomyopathy, so a normal tracing will almost rule the diagnosis out.
It confirms early disease
A normal tracing does not confirm anything; because the electrocardiogram is usually abnormal in this disease, a normal one argues strongly against it.
It points to alcohol
The electrocardiogram cannot identify alcohol as the cause. Its value here is negative: a normal tracing almost rules dilated cardiomyopathy out.

set2.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following cardiomyopathies: 2. Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: Which history precedes viral myocarditis?
opts: A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks before
Correct. Viral myocarditis follows a recent (1 to 2 week) flulike syndrome with fever, myalgia, fatigue, respiratory symptoms or gastroenteritis before the heart failure symptoms.
Chest trauma 1 to 2 days before
Trauma is not the setting. The history is a flulike viral prodrome in the 1 to 2 weeks before heart failure symptoms.
Years of heavy alcohol intake
Long-term excess alcohol causes dilated cardiomyopathy. Viral myocarditis follows a recent flulike illness.
An emotional shock hours before
An emotional stressor precedes stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy. Viral myocarditis follows a flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks earlier.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy 3. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 4. Dilated cardiomyopathy 5. Stress cardiomyopathy 6. Myocarditis
set2.q: Why are nitrates avoided in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: They cause complete heart block
Heart block is not the concern. Nitrates lower preload and afterload, which aggravates the outflow obstruction.
They raise the blood pressure
Nitrates lower rather than raise pressure; the reduced preload and afterload worsen outflow obstruction.
They thicken the septum further
Nitrates do not change wall thickness. They are avoided because reducing preload and afterload aggravates obstruction.
They worsen outflow obstruction
Correct. Drugs that reduce preload or afterload, such as nitrates, may increase symptoms by aggravating outflow tract obstruction, so they are avoided if possible.

set2.q: Why does squatting soften the murmur of obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: It slows the heart to a stop
Squatting does not act through heart rate here. It increases venous return and preload, widening the outflow tract.
It closes the mitral valve early
Early mitral closure is not the mechanism. The larger ventricular volume on squatting reduces the obstruction.
More filling reduces obstruction
Correct. Anything that increases blood flow in the heart reduces the murmur by reducing outflow obstruction; squatting and passive leg raising increase preload.
Less filling increases obstruction
Less filling makes the murmur louder, as with Valsalva or standing. Squatting does the opposite by increasing preload.

set2.q: Which condition must be differentiated from restrictive cardiomyopathy because the presentations are similar?
opts: Takotsubo syndrome
Stress cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome. The restrictive lookalike is constrictive pericarditis.
Constrictive pericarditis

Correct. Constrictive pericarditis must be differentiated because its presenting symptoms are similar; acute pericarditis, tamponade, valvular disease and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy complete the list.
Aortic dissection
Dissection is not in this differential. Constrictive pericarditis is the condition that must be separated from restrictive disease.
Viral pneumonia
Pneumonia is not on the list. Constrictive pericarditis is the lookalike that must be differentiated.

set2.q: How is the diagnosis of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy confirmed?
opts: Electrocardiogram changes
ST elevation and T wave inversion look like acute coronary syndrome; they do not confirm the diagnosis. Catheterization does.
Catheterization, normal coronaries
Correct. The diagnosis is confirmed by cardiac catheterization, which most often shows normal coronary arteries despite the wall-motion abnormality and elevated troponin.
Endomyocardial biopsy results
Biopsy is the gold standard for myocarditis, not the confirmatory test here, which is catheterization showing normal coronaries.
Troponin level above normal
Troponin is usually elevated but is not specific; it cannot separate stress cardiomyopathy from an infarct. Catheterization confirms it.

set2.q: Adverse ventricular remodeling in dilated cardiomyopathy gives the heart which shape?
opts: Narrow and tubular
A narrow tubular heart is not the remodeling pattern. Dilated cardiomyopathy produces the opposite: a globular, round heart with enlarged chambers.
Normal-sized, big atria
Normal ventricles with large atria belong to restrictive cardiomyopathy, where stiff ventricles make both atria enlarge from impaired filling.
Thick septal bulge
A bulging, thick septum is the classic pattern of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not the globular remodeling that dilated cardiomyopathy produces.
Globular, or round
Correct. Adverse ventricular remodeling leads to a globular (globe or round) shaped heart, with an increase in total cardiac mass and dilated chambers.

set2.q: What is the mainstay of treatment for acute myocarditis?
opts: Supportive care
Correct. Treatment is directed at the clinical scenario and supportive care is the mainstay, with aggressive hemodynamic stabilization when needed and drugs as required.
Septal ablation
Alcohol septal ablation treats obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Myocarditis is managed with supportive care.
Early transplant
Transplant is not the mainstay; most mild cases recover completely. Supportive care is the mainstay of treatment.
Long antibiotics
Most myocarditis is viral, and antibiotics are not the mainstay. Treatment is supportive, directed at the clinical scenario.

set2.q: What is the etiology of Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Plaque rupture
Plaque rupture is absent by definition; angiographic coronary disease is not found. The etiology is unknown.
Viral infection
Viral infection is the presumed commonest cause of myocarditis. Stress cardiomyopathy has an unknown etiology.
Unknown
Correct. The etiology of stress cardiomyopathy is unknown; what is known is that a significant emotional or physical stressor precedes it.
Amyloid
Amyloid infiltration causes restrictive cardiomyopathy. The etiology of stress cardiomyopathy is unknown.

set2.q: Which laboratory marker indicates cardiac myonecrosis in acute myocarditis?
opts: Serum amylase
Amylase is a pancreatic enzyme. Cardiac myonecrosis in myocarditis is indicated by troponin.
Serum troponin
Correct. Serum troponin is the indicator of cardiac myonecrosis; the work-up also includes a blood count for leukocytosis and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate, which may be elevated.
Serum lipase
Lipase reflects pancreatic injury, not heart muscle necrosis. Troponin is the myonecrosis marker.
Serum ferritin
Ferritin relates to iron stores, relevant to hemochromatosis, not to myonecrosis. Troponin marks myocardial necrosis.

set2.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing acute myocarditis?
opts: Serum troponin level
Troponin indicates myonecrosis but is not specific; the gold standard for myocarditis is endomyocardial biopsy.
Electrocardiogram
The electrocardiogram may show sinus tachycardia or arrhythmias; it cannot establish myocarditis. Biopsy is the gold standard.
Endomyocardial biopsy
Correct. Endomyocardial biopsy is the gold standard, used to establish the diagnosis once other causes of heart failure have been excluded.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization and angiography rule out coronary ischemia; they do not establish myocarditis, for which biopsy is the gold standard.

set2.q: Which storage disorder deposits iron in heart tissue and causes restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is inflammatory, forming granulomas in heart tissue, not an iron storage disease.
Wilson disease
Wilson disease is copper overload, not a listed cause here. The iron storage cause is hemochromatosis.
Hemochromatosis
Correct. Hemochromatosis is the storage disorder that deposits iron in heart tissue, one of the causes of restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Amyloidosis
Amyloidosis is an infiltrative disorder that deposits amyloid protein, not iron, although it is the commonest cause.

set2.q: Where are patients with Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy admitted?
opts: Home, no admission
Discharge is unsafe when the syndrome cannot be told from acute coronary syndrome early. Patients are admitted to cardiology.
To general surgery
No surgical treatment applies. Patients are admitted to cardiology and managed as acute coronary syndrome at first.
To cardiology
Correct. Because the syndrome mimics acute coronary syndrome with no reliable early differences, patients follow acute coronary syndrome protocols and are admitted to cardiology.
To psychiatry
The trigger is often emotional, but the condition is a cardiac syndrome that mimics acute coronary syndrome; admission is to cardiology.

set2.q: Which drug pair should every patient with dilated cardiomyopathy receive, whatever the cause?
opts: Beta blocker and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor

Correct. Treatment of dilated cardiomyopathy is essentially that of chronic heart failure, and all patients, regardless of etiology, should get a beta blocker and an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
Calcium channel blocker and long-acting nitrate agent
Neither is the core pair. Nitrates treat pulmonary edema in selected patients; the pair every patient receives is a beta blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
Anticoagulant and antiplatelet agent for every patient
Anticoagulation is restricted to atrial fibrillation, artificial valves or mural thrombus. The universal pair is a beta blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.
Thiazide diuretic and oral potassium supplementation
Diuretics are adjuncts for sodium and water retention, and loop diuretics are the mainstay. The universal pair is a beta blocker with an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor.

set2.q: What is the leading cause of mortality in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Endocarditis
Valve infection is not the main killer here. Sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality.
Sudden cardiac death
Correct. The clinical course varies and heart failure symptoms gradually progress, but sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of mortality in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Aortic dissection
Dissection is not a complication of this disease. Sudden cardiac death, mostly ventricular fibrillation, leads mortality.
Embolic stroke
Stroke is a risk with atrial fibrillation and is prevented with anticoagulation, but sudden cardiac death is the leading cause of death.

set2.q: Why are both atria enlarged in restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Leaking mitral leaflets
Secondary regurgitation can develop later, but the bilateral atrial enlargement comes from impaired ventricular filling.
Septal outflow blockage
Outflow obstruction is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. In restrictive disease the atria enlarge because the ventricles fill poorly.
Fluid around the heart
Pericardial fluid is tamponade, a differential diagnosis. The atria enlarge from impaired ventricular filling.
Impaired ventricular filling
Correct. Stiff ventricular walls impair diastolic filling, so both atria enlarge, and atrial fibrillation is common.

set2.q: When is an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator indicated in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Any reduced ejection fraction at diagnosis
The device is not placed at diagnosis. The threshold is an ejection fraction below 35% that persists after maximum medical therapy.
After a first episode of atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation calls for rate or rhythm care and anticoagulation, not automatically a defibrillator. The indication is ejection fraction below 35% after maximal therapy.
When the pulse pressure becomes narrow
A narrow pulse pressure reflects low stroke volume but is not a device threshold. The defibrillator threshold is ejection fraction below 35% on maximal therapy.
Ejection fraction below 35% on maximal therapy
Correct. An implantable cardioverter-defibrillator is placed if the ejection fraction is below 35% after maximum medical therapy; a biventricular device combines it with pacing.

set2.q: Where do prominent Q waves appear on the electrocardiogram in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: No lead shows Q waves
Q waves are a recognized finding, prominent in the inferior and lateral leads, along with hypertrophy and left axis deviation.
Inferior and lateral leads
Correct. Prominent Q waves appear in the inferior (II, III, aVF) and lateral (I, aVL, V4 to V6) leads, reflecting septal depolarization of hypertrophied tissue, with left axis deviation.
Right precordial leads only
The Q waves are not confined to the right precordial leads; they appear inferiorly (II, III, aVF) and laterally (I, aVL, V4 to V6).
Anterior leads V1 to V3 only
The pattern described is inferior and lateral, not anterior. It reflects septal depolarization of hypertrophied myocardium.

set2.q: What is systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve?
opts: Valve ring stretching as the ventricle dilates
A stretched ring from ventricular dilation causes the functional mitral regurgitation of dilated cardiomyopathy, not systolic anterior motion.
Leaflets thickened by old rheumatic scarring
Rheumatic scarring thickens leaflets and causes stenosis. Systolic anterior motion is a dynamic pull of the anterior leaflet into the outflow tract.
Anterior leaflet pulled into the outflow tract
Correct. High-velocity turbulent flow pulls the anterior mitral leaflet into the flow tract, causing mid-systolic obstruction of the left ventricular outflow tract and mitral regurgitation.
Posterior leaflet prolapsing into the atrium
Leaflet prolapse into the atrium is mitral valve prolapse. Systolic anterior motion drags the anterior leaflet toward the outflow tract.

set2.q: What is the first principle of managing restrictive cardiomyopathy?
opts: Surgical septal myectomy
Myectomy relieves outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; restrictive disease is managed by treating its cause.
High-dose diuresis first
Aggressive diuresis drops the preload stiff ventricles depend on. The first principle is treating the underlying disorder.
Immediate transplantation
Transplantation is the last resort, not the first principle; the underlying disorder is treated first.
Treat the underlying disorder
Correct. Management begins by treating the underlying disorder, then diuretics with caution for congestion, rate-slowing drugs, anticoagulation and pacing as needed.

set2.q: What produces the third heart sound in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Mitral leaflet striking the septum
The anterior mitral leaflet moving toward the septum is systolic anterior motion in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which causes obstruction, not a gallop.
Blood striking a compliant ventricle
Correct. The third heart sound gallop comes from a large amount of blood striking a very compliant left ventricle, a sign of volume overload.
Atrium contracting on a stiff ventricle
An atrium contracting against a stiff, noncompliant ventricle gives the fourth heart sound, as in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Closure of a thickened aortic valve
Aortic valve closure makes part of the second heart sound. The gallop of dilated cardiomyopathy is a third sound from volume overload.

set2.q: Which description fits the ventricles in dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Stiff, with near-normal cavity size
Stiff walls with reasonably preserved chamber size describe restrictive cardiomyopathy, which impairs diastolic filling while systolic function stays near normal.
Ballooned apex that later recovers
A transient ballooned, hypokinetic apex is stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, which usually recovers completely rather than progressing like dilated disease.
Dilated, with impaired contraction
Correct. Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by dilation and impaired contraction of one or both ventricles, which leads to systolic dysfunction.
Thick-walled, with a small cavity
A thick wall around a small cavity is the pattern of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, where the problem is diastolic filling rather than a weak squeeze.

set2.q: What does gadolinium add to magnetic resonance imaging in suspected myocarditis?
opts: Rules out coronary blockage
Excluding coronary ischemia is the role of cardiac angiography, not gadolinium magnetic resonance imaging.
Measures troponin release
Troponin is a blood test for myonecrosis. Gadolinium imaging shows the extent of inflammation.
Grows the causative virus
Imaging cannot culture a virus. Gadolinium improves visibility of inflammation and its extent.
Shows the extent of inflammation
Correct. Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging improves visibility and shows the extent of myocardial inflammation.

set2.q: What is the risk factor for Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: A major emotional or physical stressor
Correct. The risk factor is a significant emotional or physical stressor: death of a loved one, bad financial news, natural disaster, new illness, surgery, drug withdrawal or near drowning.
Many traditional cardiac risk factors
Patients tend to have low or no cardiac risk factors such as hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes or smoking.
A flulike illness 1 to 2 weeks before
A viral prodrome precedes myocarditis. Stress cardiomyopathy follows a significant emotional or physical stressor.
Inherited sarcomere gene mutation
Sarcomere mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The etiology of stress cardiomyopathy is unknown; its trigger is a stressor.

set2.q: What happens to ejection fraction in late-stage hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: It rises above 75%
Correct. The ejection fraction is usually normal, and in late stages it is elevated above 75% because the small ventricle nearly empties to maintain output.
It falls below 25%
A very low ejection fraction describes the dilated, weakly contracting ventricle, not the small cavity of late hypertrophic disease.
It swings every beat
Beat-to-beat swings are not the described change. The small cavity nearly empties, so ejection fraction rises above 75%.
It stays at exactly 60%
Ejection fraction does not stay fixed; it is normal early and elevated above 75% in late stages.

set2.q: Which laboratory test evaluates for anemia in suspected dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Complete blood count
Correct. The initial laboratory work includes a complete blood count for anemia, a metabolic panel for electrolytes and renal function, liver function and thyroid function.
Liver function panel
Liver function tests may be elevated in alcoholic disease or hemochromatosis; the complete blood count is the test that looks for anemia.
Thyroid function tests
Thyroid function is checked in the work-up, but for thyroid disease. Anemia is found on the complete blood count.
Metabolic panel
The comprehensive metabolic panel evaluates electrolytes and renal function. Anemia is evaluated with a complete blood count.

set2.q: Which inheritance pattern is most common in familial dilated cardiomyopathy?
opts: Mitochondrial (maternal)
Maternal mitochondrial inheritance is not the common pattern. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy is usually autosomal dominant.
Autosomal dominant
Correct. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy accounts for up to 35% of cases, and autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common pattern.
Autosomal recessive
Recessive inheritance is not the usual pattern. Familial dilated cardiomyopathy is most commonly passed on in an autosomal dominant way.
X-linked recessive
X-linked inheritance is not the pattern given for familial disease; autosomal dominant inheritance is the most common, in up to 35% of cases.

set2.q: When is anticoagulation given in Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy?
opts: Never, because recovery is usual
Recovery is usual, but a left ventricular thrombus still calls for anticoagulation.
If a ventricular thrombus is present
Correct. Supportive treatment depends on presentation: anticoagulation if a left ventricular thrombus is present, diuretics if heart failure is present, and beta blockers.
For every patient at diagnosis
Anticoagulation is not universal; it is given if a left ventricular thrombus is present.
Only when coronaries are blocked
Blocked coronaries would mean another diagnosis. In stress cardiomyopathy anticoagulation is for a ventricular thrombus.

set2.q: Which condition is in the differential diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
opts: Athletic heart
Correct. The differential is aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation, left ventricular hypertrophy from hypertensive heart disease, athletic heart and restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Aortic dissection
Aortic dissection is not on this differential. Athletic heart is, because a trained heart also thickens its walls.
Takotsubo syndrome
Stress cardiomyopathy mimics acute coronary syndrome rather than hypertrophy. Athletic heart belongs in the hypertrophic differential.
Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is not in this list. The differential includes athletic heart, aortic stenosis and hypertensive heart disease.

set2.q: When is hospice referral appropriate in cardiomyopathy?
opts: End-stage cardiomyopathy
Correct. Palliative care covers symptom management, advance care planning, goals-of-care discussions and caregiver support, with hospice referral in end-stage cardiomyopathy.
At adolescent diagnosis
Adolescent care centers on genetic screening and activity restriction for high risk. Hospice referral is for end-stage disease.
After a first arrhythmia
A first arrhythmia calls for treatment and risk review, not hospice. Hospice referral is reserved for end-stage cardiomyopathy.
Once sodium is restricted
Sodium restriction is routine adult lifestyle care. Hospice referral is appropriate in end-stage cardiomyopathy.

set2.io: Identify medical care strategies for cardiomyopathies for the following populations. 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
set2.q: What is the aim of cardiac rehabilitation programs in cardiomyopathy?
opts: Reversal of thickened ventricular walls
Rehabilitation does not reverse wall thickening. Its goals are exercise tolerance and quality of life.
Replacement of all needed medications
Rehabilitation supports medication adherence rather than replacing drugs. It aims at exercise tolerance and quality of life.
Screening of relatives for gene defects
Screening relatives is a genetic task, not rehabilitation. Cardiac rehabilitation targets exercise tolerance and quality of life.
Better exercise tolerance and quality of life
Correct. Cardiac rehabilitation programs aim to improve exercise tolerance and quality of life, with education on medications, nutrition and symptom monitoring and psychological support.
